slides.title: Combining modalities
slides.body:
A multimodal model combines two or more modalities (image + text, audio + text, image + audio + text). The architectural question: **how should the modalities interact?**

Three dominant patterns:

1. **Early fusion**: combine modalities at the input layer. Both go through the same transformer.
2. **Late fusion**: process each modality independently; combine only at the output. CLIP-style.
3. **Attention-based fusion (cross-attention)**: one modality's tokens attend into another's. Asymmetric.

Each has strengths. Modern VLMs use early fusion; modern retrieval models use late fusion; some specialized architectures use cross-attention. This lesson maps the design space.

slides.title: Late fusion — CLIP
slides.body:
**Late fusion**: separate encoders for each modality; combine only at the very end (typically via dot product in a shared embedding space).

CLIP is the canonical example:
```
image → image_encoder → image_emb (d-dim)
text → text_encoder → text_emb (d-dim)
similarity = image_emb · text_emb
```

The two encoders never see each other's intermediate features. Each learns a representation; they're aligned only at the embedding level via the contrastive loss.

**Pros**:
- **Modular**: encoders can be replaced independently.
- **Indexable**: image embeddings can be precomputed; retrieval at scale is fast (just dot products against text embeddings).
- **Cheap inference**: each encoder runs once; the comparison is a single multiply.

**Cons**:
- **No fine-grained alignment**: can't say which part of the image matches which part of the text. The interaction is purely at the global representation level.
- **Limited reasoning**: 'how many cats are in this image?' is awkward — late fusion captures global semantics, not compositional structure.

Best for: retrieval, zero-shot classification, similarity-based tasks.

slides.title: Early fusion — modern VLMs
slides.body:
**Early fusion**: project both modalities into a shared token-space; feed them into one transformer that attends across modalities.

LLaVA-style:
```
image → image_encoder → image_features
image_features → linear_projection → image_tokens (in LLM token-embedding space)
text → tokenize → text_tokens
full_input = [image_tokens, text_tokens]
full_input → LLM → response_tokens
```

The LLM processes a sequence that contains both image and text tokens; self-attention naturally handles cross-modal interactions.

**Pros**:
- **Compositional reasoning**: the model can ask 'is the cat next to the dog?' — early fusion lets the relevant image regions interact with the relevant text tokens.
- **Generative**: can generate text grounded in the image.
- **Uses LLM machinery**: leverages the LLM's existing pretraining for language understanding.

**Cons**:
- **Expensive at inference**: every query reprocesses the whole multimodal sequence.
- **No retrieval support**: can't precompute image embeddings for fast similarity search.
- **Image tokens consume context**: 256-1024 image tokens eat into the LLM's context window.

Best for: VQA, instruction-following, image captioning, multimodal chat. The dominant pattern for modern VLMs.

question.question: Why is CLIP-style late fusion preferred for image search but not for visual question answering?
options: Search needs fast retrieval (precompute embeddings, dot-product scoring) which late fusion supports cleanly. Visual question answering needs compositional reasoning ('which animal is taller?') which requires fine-grained interaction between image regions and text — late fusion's single dot-product can't capture that. Early fusion's shared transformer attention is the right tool for VQA
Late fusion can't process images larger than 224×224
question.explanation: Match architecture to task. Retrieval = global similarity = late fusion's strength. Compositional reasoning = fine-grained interaction = early fusion's strength. Trying to use the wrong architecture costs accuracy: CLIP on VQA is poor; an early-fusion VLM is overkill (and slow) for billion-image retrieval. Modern systems use both: CLIP-style retrieval to surface candidate images, then a VLM for reasoning over the retrieved set.

slides.title: Cross-attention fusion — Flamingo
slides.body:
**Cross-attention fusion**: a middle ground. The LLM's main token stream stays text-only; dedicated cross-attention layers attend to image features.

Flamingo-style (DeepMind 2022):
```
image → vision_encoder → image_features
text → tokenize → text_tokens
LLM forward pass:
    for each layer:
        self_attention(text_tokens)              # standard text self-attention
        cross_attention(text_tokens, image_features)  # text attends to image
        FFN(text_tokens)
```

Key property: image features never enter the text token stream. They're a separate input that the cross-attention layers read.

**Pros**:
- **Pretrained LLM stays frozen**: the cross-attention layers are added; the original LLM is untouched. Cheaper to train.
- **Image-feature decoupling**: the image features can be processed once and accessed by all cross-attention layers.
- **Many images in one prompt**: easy to handle interleaved (text, image, text, image) inputs.

**Cons**:
- **More parameters**: cross-attention layers add up.
- **More complex**: the architecture has more moving parts.

Flamingo, BLIP-2, and Gemini Pro use variants. Open-source has mostly converged on early-fusion (token concat, LLaVA-style) because of its simplicity, but Flamingo's design is conceptually clean and resurfaces in research.

slides.title: Fusion in practice: choosing for your task
slides.body:
A practical decision tree:

**Retrieval / similarity** (image search, deduplication, classification): **late fusion (CLIP-style)**. Precompute embeddings; index for fast lookup. The dominant pattern for any task where you need to compare against many candidates.

**VQA / reasoning / chat**: **early fusion (token concat)**. The LLM handles cross-modal attention; reuses its pretraining. LLaVA, Qwen-VL, Idefics. The default for open-source VLMs.

**Long-context multimodal** (interleaved images + text, video + text): **cross-attention (Flamingo-style)** or hybrid. Image features are kept separate from text to manage context length. Frontier multimodal (Gemini, GPT-4V at long inputs) uses some variant.

**Generation** (text-to-image, image-to-text): typically a separate generative architecture (diffusion for image generation, autoregressive LLM for caption generation), but the conditioning often uses cross-attention internally.

**Multi-stage pipelines**: retrieve with late fusion, then reason with early fusion. This is what most production multimodal apps do — index millions of images with CLIP, then run VLM reasoning on the top-k retrieved.

question.question: What's the typical recipe for production-scale multimodal applications (e.g., 'find images and explain them')?
options: Hybrid: late fusion (CLIP-style) for retrieval at scale, then early fusion (VLM) for reasoning over the top-k retrieved. The two fusion strategies have complementary strengths — retrieval needs fast indexing, reasoning needs fine-grained attention. Most production multimodal apps use this two-stage pattern
question.explanation: Hybrid pipelines exploit each fusion type for what it's good at. CLIP gives sub-second retrieval over a million-image index. The retrieved top-k (typically 10-100) is then processed by a VLM for reasoning. This is how real multimodal search engines, document QA over images, and most enterprise multimodal apps work. Pure CLIP can't reason; pure VLM can't index at scale; hybrid wins.

slides.title: What's next
slides.body:
Fusion is the architectural decision. The final lesson covers evaluation — how do you measure whether a multimodal model is any good?

Next: [[multimodal-evaluation]] — VQA benchmarks, hallucination, eval methodology.

Key takeaways:
- Late fusion (CLIP): independent encoders + similarity. Best for retrieval
- Early fusion (LLaVA): unified transformer over both modalities. Best for reasoning
- Cross-attention (Flamingo): image features kept separate; dedicated cross-attention layers. Best for long-context
- Match architecture to task; don't reach for the most powerful pattern when a simpler one fits
- Production typically uses hybrid pipelines: CLIP retrieval + VLM reasoning

slides.title: Three fusion architectures
slides.body:
**Early fusion**: concatenate raw inputs / low-level features. Forces the network to learn cross-modal interactions from scratch. Used in older multimodal work; rarely competitive today.

**Late fusion**: separately encode each modality, combine at the final embedding (often by concatenation or averaging). Simple, but loses fine-grained cross-modal interactions. CLIP is essentially late fusion at the contrastive-similarity step.

**Attention-based fusion** (cross-attention): each modality has its own encoder; cross-attention layers let each modality's tokens attend to the other's. Allows fine-grained interaction: 'this image patch is the subject mentioned in word 3'. Dominant in modern VLMs (LLaVA, BLIP-2, Flamingo).

Flamingo's pattern: frozen LLM + frozen vision encoder + small learned cross-attention 'Perceiver' modules. Add minimal parameters; the LLM consumes both text and image tokens; the LLM learns to do visual reasoning via cross-attention to image tokens.

Grounding (the model can point to *which* image region the answer refers to) is generally weaker in late-fusion than in attention-fusion architectures, because the latter has the bandwidth to express region-token correspondences. SAM + LLaVA-style assemblies achieve explicit grounding by stacking specialized models.

question.question: Cross-attention between modalities is more powerful than concatenation because:
options: It allows fine-grained token-to-token interactions between modalities, not just global combinations.
It eliminates the need for an image encoder.
question.explanation: Cross-attention lets each text token attend to specific image tokens (and vice versa). The result: 'this word is grounded to this image region', which concatenation can't express. Concatenation just stacks the modalities' final representations together; the model loses access to per-token interactions.

hints: Compare bandwidth: concatenation = one fused vector; cross-attention = N×M token interactions.
Granularity of cross-modal interaction is the key axis.
slides.workedSolution: Cross-attention provides a token-by-token interaction matrix: text token $i$ can attend to image token $j$, allowing the model to ground specific words to specific regions. Concatenation just stacks the modalities' final pooled representations together — the model can mix them globally but can't make per-token references. Most modern multimodal grounding capabilities come from this cross-attention bandwidth.

question.question: Spatial grounding
question.prompt: A VQA model is asked 'which person is wearing a red hat?'. It answers 'the person on the left' correctly, but it can't point to the bounding box. Why is this a fusion-architecture limitation, and what modification would add grounding?
Explain in two sentences why late fusion is the simplest but weakest fusion approach for VQA, while end-to-end attention fusion is the most expressive but harder to train.
question.rubric: Mentions that late fusion combines independently-encoded representations and so loses fine-grained correspondences; attention fusion provides token-by-token correspondences but needs much more co-trained data.

objectives: Distinguish early, late, and attention-based fusion.
Explain how cross-attention enables modality fusion.
